## Introduction

<!--
In chapter (connected nouns) we studied the use of
[مَا]{.ar} "what",
[مَنْ]{.ar} "who",
and
[أَيّ]{.ar} "which"
as the general connected nouns.
In this chapter, we will study the use of these same nouns as _question nouns_.

There are other question nouns besides the ones above, like
[كَيْفَ]{.ar} "how",
[أَيْنَ]{.ar} "where"
[مَتَىٰ]{.ar} "when".
There are also question-devices which are particles, not nouns, like
[أَ]{.ar}
and
[هَلْ]{.ar}.
We will study all these elsewhere, if Allāh wills.
-->

Questions in Arabic are introduced by
_question-devices_.
Question-devices can be particles like
[أَ]{.ar} and [هَلْ]{.ar} used to introduce yes/no questions.
Or they can be nouns like:

+ [مَا]{.ar} [what]{.trans}
+ [مَنْ]{.ar} [who]{.trans}
+ [أَيّ]{.ar} [which]{.trans}
+ [كَيْفَ]{.ar} [how]{.trans}
+ [أَيْنَ]{.ar} [where]{.trans}
+ [مَتَىٰ]{.ar} [when]{.trans}

Question-devices occur in the beginnning of a question sentence.
We will study these and other question-devices in this chapter, if Allāh wills.


## [أَ]{.ar} and [هَلْ]{.ar}

### [أَ]{.ar}

[أَ]{.ar} is the most basic question-device.
It is used to form:

1. Yes-no questions. For example:

   (@) [أَحَضَرَ القَاضِي]{.ar}
       [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271]{.citex}  
       [Has the judge come?]{.trans}  

2. Multiple-choice questions. For example:

   (@) [أَمُحَمَّدٌ عِنْدَكَ أَمْ خَالِدٌ]{.ar}
       [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271]{.citex}  
       [Is [#muHammad]{.trn2} with you or [#xAlid]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

Here are some examples of yes/no questions using [أَ]{.ar}:

(@) [أَصَلَّى النَّاسُ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :687](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:687)]{.citex}  
    [Have the people prayed?]{.trans}  

(@) [أَتَرْضَوْنَ أَنْ يَذْهَبَ النَّاسُ بِالشَّاةِ وَالْبَعِيرِ، وَتَذْهَبُونَ بِالنَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم إِلَى رِحَالِكُمْ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :4330](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4330)]{.citex}  
    [Are you pleased that the people are going away with sheep and camels, while you are going with the Prophet [ﷺ]{.areng} to your homes?]{.trans}  

(@) [قَالُوۤا۟ ءَأَنتَ فَعَلۡتَ هَـٰذَا بِـَٔالِهَتِنَا یَـٰۤإِبۡرَ ٰ⁠هِیمُ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:62](https://quran.com/21/62)]{.citex}  
    [They said, "Have you done this to our gods, O Abraham?"]{.trans}  

(@) [أَمَا تَسْتَحِي مِنَ اللهِ]{.ar}  
    [Wright 2/307A]{.citex}  
    [Aren't you ashamed from Allāh?]{.trans}  

(@) [أَلَمْ أُرْسِلْ إِلَيْكَ رَسُولاً]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :1413](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1413)]{.citex}  
    [Didn't I send a messenger to you?]{.trans}  

Exceptionally,
when
conjunctions like [وَ]{.ar}, [فَ]{.ar}, and [ثُمَّ]{.ar} are to be added before the question,
they will follow [أَ]{.ar}, not precede it.
For example:

(@) [فَقَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ أَوَكُلُّكُمْ رَأْيُهُ عَلَى هَذَا]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/307A]{.citex}  
    [[#abU]{.trn2} Bakr said, "Are all of you of this opinion?"]{.trans}  

(@) [أَفَتَدْرُونَ أَىُّ شَهْرٍ هَذَا]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :1742](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1742)]{.citex}  
    [Do you then know which month this is?]{.trans}  

(@) [أَثُمَّ إِذَا مَا وَقَعَ ءَامَنتُم بِهِۦۤۚ ءَاۤلۡـَٔـٰنَ وَقَدۡ كُنتُم بِهِۦ تَسۡتَعۡجِلُونَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة يونس]{.ar} 10:51](https://quran.com/10/51)]{.citex}  
    [Then is it that when it has [actually] occurred you will believe in it? Now? And you were [once] for it impatient.]{.trans}  

When the word following [أَ]{.ar} is a nound beginning with a
connecting hamzah,
then [أَ]{.ar} may replace the connecting hamzah.
For example:

(@) [أَبْنُكَ ...]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/24A]{.citex}  
    [Is your son ...?]{.trans}  
    (instead of [أَٱبْنُكَ]{.ar}.)

(@) [أَنْكَسَرَتْ]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/24A]{.citex}  
    [Did it break?]{.trans}  
    (instead of [أَٱنْكَسَرَتْ]{.ar}.)

(@) [أَلْمَاءُ ...]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/24B]{.citex}  
    [Is the water ...?]{.trans}  
    (instead of [أَٱلْمَاءُ]{.ar}.)

When [أَ]{.ar} precedes [ال]{.ar},
as in example () above,
then the two alifs may also be combined to form
[آ]{.ar}.
So we can also say:

(@) [آلْمَاءُ ...]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/24B]{.citex}  
    [Is the water ...?]{.trans}  
    (instead of [أَٱلْمَاءُ]{.ar} or [أَلْمَاءُ]{.ar}.)

Similarly,

(@) [آلْحَسَنُ عِنْدَكَ]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/24B]{.citex}  
    [Is [al-#Hasan]{.trn2} with you?]{.trans}  
    (instead of [أَٱلْحَسَنُ]{.ar}.)

(@) [آلْقُرَشِيُّ أَمْ الثَّقَفِيُّ عِنْدَكَ]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/24B]{.citex}  
    [Is [he] of [#qurayc]{.trn2} or of [#vaqIf]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

### [أَمْ]{.ar} vs [أَوْ]{.ar}

[أَمْ]{.ar} is used to provide options in multiple-choice questions
when the answer is _either_ one _or_ another of the provided options.
For example, in the question:

(@) [أَمُحَمَّدٌ عِنْدَكَ أَمْ خَالِدٌ]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271]{.citex}  
    [Is [#muHammad]{.trn2} with you or [#xAlid]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

The answer can only be either
[[#muHammad]{.trn2}]{.trans}.
or
[[#xAlid]{.trn2}]{.trans}.
Similarly, if we say:

(@) [أَزَيْدٌ أَفْضَلُ أَمْ خَالِدٌ]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/296 citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [Is Zayd better or [#xAlid]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

The answer can only be either
[Zayd]{.trans}
or
[[#xAlid]{.trn2}]{.trans}.

[أَوْ]{.ar},
on the other hand,
is used in yes/no questions.
For examples:

(@) [أَلَقِيتَ زَيْدًا أَوْ عَمْرًا أَوْ خَالِدًا]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/295 citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [Did you meet Zayd or [#eamr]{.trn2} or [#xAlid]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

(@) [أَعِنْدَكَ زَيْدٌ أَوْ خَالِدٌ أَوْ عَمْرٌو]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/295 citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [Is Zayd or [#xAlid]{.trn2} or [#eamr]{.trn2} with you?]{.trans}  

then we are asking if you met _any_ one of the named persons,
and if any of them are with you.
So the answer can be [yes]{.trans} or [no]{.trans}.

Here is another scenario where [أَمْ]{.ar} is contrasted with [أَوْ]{.ar}.
Consider the following examples:

(@) [مَا أَدْرِي أَأَكَلَ أَمْ شَرِبَ]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/296]{.citex}  
    [I don't know: did he eat or [or did he] drink.]{.trans}  

(@) [مَا أَدْرِي أَأَكَلَ أَوْ شَرِبَ]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/296]{.citex}  
    [I don't know: did he eat or drank.]{.trans}  

In the first example, you are wondering which of the two options he did.
Whereas in the second example, you are wondering if he did any of the two examples.

### [أَمْ]{.ar} as a question-device

[أَمْ]{.ar} is also used as a question-device on its own right,
when asking a yes/no question as an alternative.
For example:


(@) [هَلْ لك قبلنا حق **أم** أنت رَجُل معروفٌ بالظلم]{.ar}
    [[[معاني القرآن للفراء]{.ar} 1/72](https://shamela.ws/book/23634/85) cited by [[مغني اللبيب لابن هشام]{.ar} 1/289](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/55330/read?page=241&part=1#p-55330-241-2)]{.citex}  
    [Do you have a right before us, **or** are you a man known for transgression?]{.trans}  

Similarly,

(@) [قُلۡ هَلۡ یَسۡتَوِی ٱلۡأَعۡمَىٰ وَٱلۡبَصِیرُ أَمۡ هَلۡ تَسۡتَوِی ٱلظُّلُمَـٰتُ وَٱلنُّورُۗ أَمۡ جَعَلُوا۟ لِلَّهِ شُرَكَاۤءَ خَلَقُوا۟ كَخَلۡقِهِۦ فَتَشَـٰبَهَ ٱلۡخَلۡقُ عَلَیۡهِمۡۚ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الرعد]{.ar} 13:16](https://quran.com/13/16) cited by [[مغني اللبيب لابن هشام]{.ar} 1/289](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/55330/read?page=241&part=1#p-55330-241-2)]{.citex}  
    [Say, "Is the blind equivalent to the seeing? Or is darkness equivalent to light? Or have they attributed to Allāh partners who created like His creation so that the creation [of each] seemed similar to them?"]{.trans}  

(@) [أَمۡ لَهُ ٱلۡبَنَـٰتُ وَلَكُمُ ٱلۡبَنُونَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الطور]{.ar} 52:39](https://quran.com/52/39) cited by [[مغني اللبيب لابن هشام]{.ar} 1/289](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/55330/read?page=241&part=1#p-55330-241-2)]{.citex}  
    [Or has He daughters while you have sons?]{.trans}  


### Omitting [أَ]{.ar}

[أَ]{.ar} may frequently be omitted from a question sentence.
Its meaning will then be implicit.
For example:

(@) [فَوَاللهِ مَا أَدْرِي وَإِنْ كُنْتُ دَارِيًا بِسَبْعٍ رَمَيْنَ الْجَمْرَ أَمْ بِثَمَانٍ]{.ar}
    [cited by [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 237](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1342)]{.citex}  
    [By Allāh, I don't know, even though I am knowledgeable, with seven did they throw the pebbles or with eight?]{.trans}  
    (for [أَبِسَبْعٍ]{.ar})

Similarly:

(@) [وَجَاۤءَ ٱلسَّحَرَةُ فِرۡعَوۡنَ قَالُوۤا۟ إِنَّ لَنَا لَأَجۡرًا إِن كُنَّا نَحۡنُ ٱلۡغَـٰلِبِینَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأعراف]{.ar} 7:113](https://quran.com/7/113) [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 237](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1342)]{.citex}  
    [And the magicians came to Pharaoh. They said, "Indeed for us is a reward if we are the predominant."]

### [هَلْ]{.ar}

[هَلْ]{.ar} is similar to [أَ]{.ar} in that it introduced yes/no questions.
Here are some examples with [هَلْ]{.ar}:

(@) [هَلۡ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِیثُ ٱلۡجُنُودِ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة البروج]{.ar} 85:17](https://quran.com/85/17) cited by Wright 2/308C]{.citex}  
    [Has there reached you the story of the soldiers -]{.trans}  

(@) [یَـٰۤأَیُّهَا ٱلَّذِینَ ءَامَنُوا۟ هَلۡ أَدُلُّكُمۡ عَلَىٰ تِجَـٰرَةࣲ تُنجِیكُم مِّنۡ عَذَابٍ أَلِیمࣲ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الصف]{.ar} 61:10](https://quran.com/61/10) cited by Wright 2/308C]{.citex}  
    [O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?]{.trans}  

(@) [هَلْ أَنْتُمْ تَارِكُو لِي صَاحِبِي]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :4640](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4640) cited by Wright 2/308C]{.citex}  
    [Are you (people) leaving for me my companion?]{.trans}  

### [هَلْ]{.ar} vs [أَ]{.ar}

[هَلْ]{.ar} or [أَ]{.ar} are often interchangeable,
but there are also some differences between them.
[أَ]{.ar} is more basic and direct,
whereas
[هَلْ]{.ar} will add more wonder, liveliness, or incredulity to the question.^[Wright 2/308C],
Unlike [أَ]{.ar}, [هَلْ]{.ar} cannot be used for multiple-choice questions.

Here are some more differences between [هَلْ]{.ar} and [أَ]{.ar}:

Unlike [أَ]{.ar},
the conjunctions
[وَ]{.ar}, [فَ]{.ar}, and [ثُمَّ]{.ar} do precede [هَلْ]{.ar} when needed.
For example:

(@) [وَهَلۡ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِیثُ مُوسَىٰۤ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة طه]{.ar} 20:9](https://quran.com/20/9) cited by Wright 2/308D]{.citex}  
    [And has the story of Moses reached you? -]{.trans}  

(@) [إِنْ أَقَمْتُ إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ فَهَلْ أَنْتَ رَائِحٌ مَعِي]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/308D]{.citex}  
    [If I stay till the evening, then will you go with me?]{.trans}  

[هَلْ]{.ar} cannot be prefixed to a negative clause (excepting [هَلَّا]{.ar}, see () below).
For example:

(@) ✗ [هَلْ لَمْ يَحْضُرْ أَخُوكَ]{.ar}  
    ✓ [أَلَمْ يَحْضُرْ أَخُوكَ]{.ar}  
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/283]{.citex}  
    [Didn't your brother come?]{.trans}  

(@) ✗ [هَلْ لَيْسَ أَخُوكَ حَاضِرًا]{.ar}  
    ✓ [أَلَيْسَ أَخُوكَ حَاضِرًا]{.ar}  
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/283]{.citex}  
    [Isn't your brother present?]{.trans}  

[هَلْ]{.ar} prefixed to a [muDArie]{.trn2} verb usually
(not not exclusively)
restricts the tense to the future.
For example:

(@) [هَلْ تُسَافٍرُ]{.ar}
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/283]{.citex}  
    [**Will** you journey?]{.trans}  

Occassionally, it can admit a present tense meaning.
For example:

(@) [قُلۡ یَـٰۤأَهۡلَ ٱلۡكِتَـٰبِ **هَلۡ تَنقِمُونَ مِنَّاۤ** إِلَّاۤ أَنۡ ءَامَنَّا بِٱللَّهِ وَمَاۤ أُنزِلَ إِلَیۡنَا وَمَاۤ أُنزِلَ مِن قَبۡلُ وَأَنَّ أَكۡثَرَكُمۡ فَـٰسِقُونَ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة المائدة]{.ar} 5:59](https://quran.com/5/59) cited by [معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/283]{.citex}  
    [Say, "O People of the Scripture, **do you resent us** except [for the fact] that we have believed in Allāh and what was revealed to us and what was revealed before and because most of you are defiantly disobedient?"]{.trans}  

[هَلْ]{.ar} is not prefixed to a conditional-device.
For example:

(@) ✗ [هَلْ إِنْ سَافَرَ سَافَرْتَ مَعَهُ]{.ar}  
    ✓ [أَإِنْ سَافَرَ سَافَرْتَ مَعَهُ]{.ar}  
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/284]{.citex}  
    [If he journeys, will you journey with him?]{.trans}  

[هَلْ]{.ar} is not prefixed to a [إِنَّ]{.ar}.
For example:

(@) ✗ [هَلْ إِنَّهُ شَاعِرٌ]{.ar}  
    ✓ [أَإِنَّهُ شَاعِرٌ]{.ar}  
    [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/284]{.citex}  
    [Is he indeed a poet?]{.trans}  

[هَلْ]{.ar} is not prefixed to a noun, following which is a verb indicating a choice or alternative.
For example:

(@) ✗ [هَلْ خَالِدٌ يَرْجِعُ]{.ar}  
    ✓ [أَخَالِدٌ يَرْجِعُ]{.ar}  
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/243](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1348)]{.citex}  
    [Is it [#xAlid]{.trn2} returning?]{.trans}  

(@) ✗ [هَلْ خَالِدًا أَكْرَمْتَ]{.ar}  
    ✓ [أَخَالِدًا أَكْرَمْتَ]{.ar}  
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/243](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1348)]{.citex}  
    [Is it [#xAlid]{.trn2} you honored?]{.trans}  

[هَلْ]{.ar} is used in an exceptive question sentence
that gives the meaning of a negative sentence.
[أَ]{.ar} is not used in this manner.
For example:

(@) ✓ [هَلْ حَضَرَ إِلَّا مُحَمَّدٌ]{.ar}
    ✗ [أَحَضَرَ إِلَّا مُحَمَّدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/243](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1348)]{.citex}  
    [Did anyone come except [#muHammad]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  
    (i.e. [No one came except [#muHammad]{.trn2}.]{.trans})  

Also, [أَ]{.ar} because of its direct nature can imply that the action being asked about was done or is being done.
[هَلْ]{.ar} has no such implication.^[[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/247](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1352)]
For example:

(@) [أَتَضْرِبُ زَيدًا]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/247](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1352) citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [Are you beating Zayd?]{.trans}  
    (The implication could be that you _are_ beating him and the question is in response to your action.)

(@) [هَلْ تَضْرِبُ زَيدًا]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/247](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1352) citing [كتاب سيبويه]{.ar}]{.citex}  
    [Are you beating Zayd?]{.trans}  
    (There is no implication you are beating him.)

Similarly,

(@) [أَحَضَرَ خَالِدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/248](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1353)]{.citex}  
    [Did [#xAlid]{.trn2} come?]{.trans}  
    (The implication could be that you expected [#xAlid]{.trn2} to have come and you are confirming whether he did.)

(@) [هَلْ حَضَرَ خَالِدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/248](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1353)]{.citex}  
    [Did [#xAlid]{.trn2} come?]{.trans}  
    (There is no implication you expected [#xAlid]{.trn2} to have come.)

[هَلْ]{.ar} with the verb [تَسْتَطِيعُ]{.ar} [can]{.trans} can also be used for requests.^[See also the [tafsIr]{.trn2} of [إِذۡ قَالَ ٱلۡحَوَارِیُّونَ یَـٰعِیسَى ٱبۡنَ مَرۡیَمَ هَلۡ یَسۡتَطِیعُ رَبُّكَ أَن یُنَزِّلَ عَلَیۡنَا مَاۤىِٕدَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَاۤءِۖ]{.quran} [[[سورة المائدة]{.ar} 5:112](https://quran.com/5/112)]{.citex}]
For example:

(@) [هَلْ تَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ تُرِيَنِي كَيْفَ كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَتَوَضَّأُ]{.ar}
    [[[سنن النسائي]{.ar} :98](https://sunnah.com/nasai:98)]{.citex}  
    [Can you show me how the Messenger of Allāh [ﷺ]{.areng} would perform [wuDUE]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  


### [هَلْ لَكَ فِي]{.ar}

Wright 2/309D

### [هَلَّا]{.ar}, [أَلَا]{.ar}

Wright 310D

## Sentence word order

In a question sentence,
the noun being asked about is typically put first in sentence word order.
So, for example,
if the question sentence is led with a verb,
then it is the action of the verb which is being asked about:

(@) [أَحَضَرَ مُحَمَّدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/270](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1375)]{.citex}  
    [Did [#muHammad]{.trn2} attend?]{.trans}  
    (i.e. did [#muHammad]{.trn2}'s attending occur?)

But if the noun comes first,
then the identity of the person attending is being asked about:

(@) [أَمُحَمَّدٌ حَضَرَ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/270](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1375)]{.citex}  
    [Is it [#muHammad]{.trn2} who attended?]{.trans}  

Similarly,

<!--
(@) [قَالُوۤا۟ ءَأَنتَ فَعَلۡتَ هَـٰذَا بِـَٔالِهَتِنَا یَـٰۤإِبۡرَ ٰ⁠هِیمُ]{.quran}
    [[[سورة الأنبياء]{.ar} 21:62](https://quran.com/21/62) cited by [[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/270](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1375)]{.citex}  
    [They said, "Have you done this to our gods, O Abraham?"]{.trans}  
-->

(@) [أَأَكْرَمْتَ مُحَمَّدًا]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1376)]{.citex}  
    [Did you honor [#muHammad]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

(@) [أَمُحَمَّدًا أَكْرَمْتَ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1376)]{.citex}  
    [Is it [#muHammad]{.trn2} you honored?]{.trans}  

and

(@) [أَسَافَرَ خَالِدٌ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1376)]{.citex}  
    [Did [#xAlid]{.trn2} journey on Friday?]{.trans}  

(@) [أَيَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ سَافَرَ خَالِدٌ]{.ar}
    [[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 4/271](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/1376)]{.citex}  
    [Is it on Friday [#xAlid]{.trn2} journeyed?]{.trans}  




## [مَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ]{.ar}

### Position in the beginning of the question sentence

All question-devices typically occur in the beginning of the question sentence.
(Particles like [وَ]{.ar}, [فَ]{.ar}, etc. are allowed to precede them.)
For example,

(@) [مَنْ أَنْتَ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/311D]{.citex}  
    [Who are you?]{.trans}  

(@) [وَمَا تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ؟]{.ar}
    [[[سورة طه]{.ar} 20:17](https://quran.com/20:17)]{.citex}  
    [And what is that in your right hand?]{.trans}  

In both the above examples, the question nouns
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar}
are in the u-case as the subject of their respective question sentences.

When the question is asking about the direct doee of a verb, then too
is the question noun placed in the beginning of the sentence. For example,

(@) [مَا تَقُولُ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/312A]{.citex}  
    [What do you say?]{.trans}  

(@) [مَنْ قَتَلْتَ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/311D]{.citex}  
    [Whom did you kill?]{.trans}  

(@) [مَا فَرَضَ رَبُّكَ عَلَىٰ أُمَّتِكَ؟]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :162a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:162a)]{.citex}  
    [What has your Lord enjoined upon your [#ummah]{.trn2}?]{.trans}  

In the above three examples, the question nouns
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar}
are analyzed as the a-case direct doee of the verb following it.

It is also possible, in such cases,
for the verb to have a pronoun direct doee.
For example:

(@istifham_man_ra2ayta) [مَنْ رَأَيْتَهُ]{.ar}
    [[[مغني اللبيب لابن هشام]{.ar} 5/436](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/55330/read?page=2488&part=5#p-55330-2488-3)]{.citex}  
    [Whom did you see?]{.trans}  
    (instead of [مَنْ رَأَيْتَ]{.ar})

In example (@istifham_man_ra2ayta) above,
[مَنْ]{.ar} can be analyzed as either a (positional) u-case subject such that the verbal sentence [رَأَيْتَهُ]{.ar} is its info,
or [مَنْ]{.ar} can be a preoccupied-from direct doee
(see (ref)).^[[[مغني اللبيب لابن هشام]{.ar} 5/436](https://ketabonline.com/ar/books/55330/read?page=2488&part=5#p-55330-2488-3)]

The question nouns are exempted from being placed in the beginning of the question noun when they are in the i-case:
either following a preposition, or as the annexed-to noun in an annexation. For example,

(@) [لِمَنْ هَـٰذَا ٱلْقَصْرُ؟]{.ar}
    [[[جامع الترمذي]{.ar} :3688](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3688)]{.citex}  
    [Whose is this palace?]{.trans}  

(@) [بِنْتُ مَنْ أَنْتِ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/311D]{.citex}  
    [Whose daughter are you?]{.trans}  

### [مَا]{.ar} shortened to [مَ]{.ar} in the i-case

When the question noun [مَا]{.ar} [mA]{.trn} is in the i-case it is typically shortened to [مَ]{.ar} [ma]{.trn}.
Example:

(@) [بِمَ يَرْجِعُ؟]{.ar}
    [[[سنن ابن ماجه]{.ar} :4108](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:4108)]{.citex}  
    [With what does he return?]{.trans}  

This shortened [مَ]{.ar} is also usually joined to the preposition before it,
even for prepositions constituting more than one letter (which don't typically join to the word directly following it).
So we get:

+ [بِمَ]{.ar} for [بِمَا]{.ar}
+ [لِمَ]{.ar} for [لِمَا]{.ar}
+ [فِيمَ]{.ar} for [فِي مَا]{.ar}
+ [إِلَامَ]{.ar} for [إِلَىٰ مَا]{.ar}
+ [عَلَامَ]{.ar} for [عَلَىٰ مَا]{.ar}
+ [حَتَّامَ]{.ar} for [حَتَّىٰ مَا]{.ar}
+ [مِمَّ]{.ar} for [مِمَّا]{.ar} ([مِنْ مَا]{.ar})
+ [عَمَّ]{.ar} for [عَمَّا]{.ar} ([عَنْ مَا]{.ar})

When pausing on this shortened [مَ]{.ar}, a [هْ]{.ar} is appended to it to preserve the sound of the [fatHah]{.trn2}.
For example:

(@) [لِمَهْ؟]{.ar}  
    [limah?]{.trn}  
    [For what?]{.trans}  

The shortened [مَ]{.ar} is also used when it is the annexed-to noun in an annexation. 
However, in this case it won't be joined to the previous word.
For example:

(@) [مِثْلُ مَ أَنْتَ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 1/275A]{.citex}  
    [What are you like?]{.trans}

### [مَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ]{.ar} referred back to with an i-case pronoun

As an alternative to placing the question noun
[مَا]{.ar}
or
[مَنْ]{.ar}
after the preposition or annexed noun,
the question noun may be placed in the beginning of the sentence
and it is referred back to by a pronoun. For example,

(@) [قُلْ مَنْ بِيَدِهِ مَلَكُوتُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ]{.ar}
    [[[سورة المؤمنون]{.ar} 23:88](https://quran.com/23:88)]{.citex}  
    [Say, "In whose hand is the realm of all things"]{.trans}  

(@) [مَاذَا يَسْتَعْجِلُ مِنْهُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ]{.ar}
    [[[سورة يونس]{.ar} 10:50](https://quran.com/10:50)]{.citex}  
    [for which [aspect] of it would the criminals be impatient?]{.trans}

### Verb gender when inquiring about the doer of a verb

The question nouns
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar}
are themselves masculine singular nouns.
But they can be used to ask about nouns of any gender or number.
For example,

(@) [وَمَا تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ؟]{.ar}
    [[[سورة طه]{.ar} 20:17](https://quran.com/20:17)]{.citex}  
    [And what is that in your right hand?]{.trans}

(@) [مَنْ هَـٰؤُلَاءِ ٱلرِّجَالُ؟]{.ar}  
    [Who are these men?]{.trans}

When inquiring about the doer of a verb, then the verb is usually construed with a masculine singular doer to match the question noun. For example:

(@) [مَنْ جَاءَ؟]{.ar}  
    [Who has come?]{.trans}

(@) [مَا يُبْكِيكَ؟]{.ar}
    [[[جامع الترمذي]{.ar} :3894](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3894)]{.citex}  
    [What makes you cry?]{.trans}

Ocassionally, the feminine verb may be used if asking about a feminine doer. For example:

(@) [مَنْ كَانَتْ أُمَّكَ؟]{.ar}
    ^[See also [[البحر المحيط لأبي حيان]{.ar} for [سورة النساء]{.ar} 4:176](https://tafsir.app/albahr-almuheet/4/176) ([فإن كانتا اثنتين]{.ar}) and [[البحر المحيط لأبي حيان]{.ar} for [سورة الأنعام]{.ar} 6:23](https://tafsir.app/albahr-almuheet/6/23) ([ثم لم تكن فتنتهم]{.ar})]
    [Wright 2/313C]{.citex}  
    [Who was your mother?]{.trans}

<!--Note how [كَانَتْ]{.ar} has a feminine doer pronoun to match the gender of [أُمَّكَ]{.ar}.-->

If the question is regarding a specific number and gender, then we are more likely to insert the corresponding specific connected noun
([ٱلَّذِي]{.ar}, etc.)
between the question noun [مَن]{.ar} and the verb. 
For example:

(@) [مَنِ اللَّتَانِ تَظَاهَرَتَا عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم مِنْ أَزْوَاجِهِ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :4913](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4913)]{.citex}  
    [Who are the ones~2f~, from his wives, who aided one another against the Prophet [ﷺ]{.areng}?]{.trans}  

Note that now the dual feminine doer pronoun [ا]{.ar} in [تَظَاهَرَتَا]{.ar} is the refer-back pronoun that refers back to the connected noun [ٱللَّتَانِ]{.ar}.

### An indefinite noun after [مَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ]{.ar}

The question nouns [مَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ]{.ar}
cannot occur as annexed nouns.
Nor can either of them be a replacee.
So any indefinite noun after them must necessarily be the info of the question sentence.
For example,
[مَنْ فَارِسٌ؟]{.ar} 
[Wright 2/312C]{.citex}
can only mean, "Who is a horseman?" not "Who horseman?" or "Which horseman?"

### [مَاذَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ ذَا]{.ar}

To lend more force to the question or to make it more lively, [ذَا]{.ar} may be appended to the question nouns
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar}.
For example,

(@) [مَاذَا قَالَ رَبُّكُمْ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :4800](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4800)]{.citex}  
    [What did your lord say?]{.trans}

With [مَنْ ذَا]{.ar} especially, but also with [مَا]{.ar}, the specific connected noun [ٱلَّذِي]{.ar} is often appended as well.
For example:

(@) [مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي قَالَ هَذَا]{.ar}
    [[[سنن ابن ماجه]{.ar} :3802](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:3802)]{.citex}  
    [Who is the one that said this?]{.trans}

(@) [مَاذَا ٱلَّذِي تَقُولُ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/312B]{.citex}  
    [What is it that you say?]{.trans}

Note that [ذَا]{.ar} is also a variant pointing noun meaning "this" or "that". 
In which case, it can be the info of the question sentence by itself.
For example:

<!--[مَنْ ذَا؟]{.ar}
"Who is that?"-->

(@) [فَدَقَقْتُ الْبَابَ، فَقَالَ: مَنْ ذَا؟ فَقُلْتُ: أَنَا، قَالَ: أَنَا، أَنَا؟، كَأَنَّهُ كَرِهَهُ.]{.ar}
    [[[الأدب المفرد]{.ar} :1086](https://sunnah.com/adab:1086)]{.citex}  
    [So I knocked at the door. He said, 'Who is that?' I said, 'I.' He said 'I? I?' as if he disliked it.]{.trans}

### Why

Arabic has no distinct question-device for "why".
Instead, the question noun [مَا]{.ar} is used with a preposition, typically [لِ]{.ar}
to give the meaning "For what?".
For example,

(@) [لِمَ فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :705b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:705b)]{.citex}  
    [Why did he do that?]{.trans}

(@) [لِمَاذَا وَلَّيْتَ بَعْدَ مَجِيِّكَ إِلَىٰ هَـٰهُنَا؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/312B]{.citex}  
    [Why did you turn back after your coming here?]{.trans}

Sometimes, other prepositions like [عَلَىٰ]{.ar} and [بِ]{.ar} may be used. But this is dependent on the verb in the sentence.
For example,

(@) [عَلَامَ يَقْتُلُ أَحَدُكُمْ أَخَاهُ]{.ar}
    [[[مشكاة المصابيح]{.ar} :4562](https://sunnah.com/mishkat:4562)]{.citex}  
    [Why does one of you kill his brother?]{.trans}  
    i.e. "on what [basis]"

(@) [بِمَ يَأْخُذ أحدكُم مَال أَخِيه؟]{.ar}
    [[[مشكاة المصابيح]{.ar} :2840](https://sunnah.com/mishkat:2840)]{.citex}  
    [Why should any of you take his brother’s property?]{.trans}  
    i.e. "by what [justification]"

And often times, the meaning "why" is conveyed using [مَا]{.ar} when a suitable verb exists. For example:

(@) [مَا يُبْكِيكَ؟]{.ar}
    [[[جامع الترمذي]{.ar} :3894](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3894)]{.citex}  
    [What makes you cry?]{.trans}  
    i.e. "Why are you crying?"

### Applicability of [مَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ]{.ar} to intelligent and non-intelligent beings {#man-and-maa-for-intelligent}

In (give ref) we discussed how, sometimes, the connected noun [مَا]{.ar} may be used for intelligent beings
and [مَنْ]{.ar} for non-intelligent beings.
Those same guidelines apply for [مَا]{.ar} and [مَنْ]{.ar} when they are question nouns.
For example,
when inquiring about the nature or qualities of a person [مَا]{.ar} may be used. Examples:

(@) [فَقُلْتُ لَهُ مَا أَنْتَ قَالَ أَنَا نَبِيٌّ. فَقُلْتُ وَمَا نَبِيٌّ قَالَ أَرْسَلَنِي اللَّهُ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :832](https://sunnah.com/muslim:832)]{.citex}  
    [I said, 'Who are you?' He said, 'I am a prophet.' So I said, 'And who is a prophet?' He said 'Allāh has sent me.']{.trans}

## [أَيّ]{.ar}

In section .. we studied [أَيّ]{.ar} as a general connected noun.
Just like
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar},
[أَيّ]{.ar}
too can be a question noun for "which" questions.
Many of the rules that apply the question nouns
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar}
also apply to 
[أَيّ]{.ar}.
For example,
the default position of 
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is in the beginning of the question sentence.

However,
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is also different from 
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar}
in some respects.
For example,
consistent with what we learned in its use as a connected noun,
the question noun
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is a fully-flexible noun
and can be used indiscriminately for both intelligent and non-intelligent beings.

Also, 
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is typically the annexed noun in an annexation.
When
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is a connected noun, then its annexed-to noun is usually definite.
But when
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is a question noun, then its annexed-to noun may be either definite or indefinite.

### [أَيّ]{.ar} with a definite annexed-to noun

When the annexed-to noun of 
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is a definite noun, the annexation has the meaning "which [one] of".
For example,

(@) [فَأَيَّ آيَاتِ ٱللَّهِ تُنكِرُونَ]{.ar}
    [[[سورة غافر]{.ar} 40:81](https://quran.com/40:81)]{.citex}  
    [So which of the signs of Allāh do you deny?]{.trans}

(@) [أَيُّ الأَعْمَالِ أَفْضَلُ]{.ar}
    [[[سنن أبي داود]{.ar} :1449](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:1449)]{.citex}  
    [Which of the deeds is best?]{.trans}

(@) [فَأَيُّ الْفَرِيقَيْنِ أَحَقُّ بِالْأَمْنِ]{.ar}
    [[[سورة الأنعام]{.ar} 6:81](https://quran.com/6/81)]{.citex}  
    [So which of the two parties has more right to security]{.trans}

(@) [مِنْ أَيِّ أَيَّامِ الشَّهْرِ كَانَ يَصُومُ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :1160](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1160)]{.citex}  
    [From which of the days of the month would he fast?]{.trans}

As in the examples above, the annexed-to noun in such a case is typically a plural or a dual.
If the annexed-to noun is a definite singular noun, then there is an implied partitive meaning,
i.e. "which part of".^[Wright 2/220A]
For example,

<!--
[أَيُّ ٱلرَّجُلِ أَحْسَنُ؟]{.ar}
"Which (aspect or feature) of the man is most handsome?"
-->

(@) [فِي أَيِّ طَعَامِهِ يُبَارَكُ لَهُ]{.ar}
    [[[سنن أبي داود]{.ar} :3845](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:3845)]{.citex}  
    [in which (part) of his food is the blessing]{.trans}

(@) [مِنْ أَيِّ الْمَالِ]{.ar}
    [[[سنن أبي داود]{.ar} :4063](https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4063)]{.citex}  
    [From which (category) of wealth?]{.trans}

However, if the noun is of generic definiteness then the partitive aspect indicates one out of the set that constitutes the generic type. In English the plural is often used to signify the generic type.
For example the generic type [ٱلْعَمَل]{.ar} "the deed" can be translated in English as "deeds".
So [أَيُّ ٱلْعَمَلِ]{.ar} means "which one from the generic type 'deeds'" or simply "which deed".
Examples:

(@) [أَيُّ الْعَمَلِ أَحَبُّ إِلَى اللهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ؟]{.ar}
    [[[الأدب المفرد]{.ar} :1](https://sunnah.com/adab:1)]{.citex}  
    [Which deed is most beloved to Allāh?]{.trans}

(@) [أَيُّ الدُّعَاءِ أَفْضَلُ]{.ar}
    [[[الأدب المفرد]{.ar} :637](https://sunnah.com/adab:637)]{.citex}  
    "Which supplication is best?"

(@) [أَيُّ الذَّنْبِ أَعْظَمُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :4477](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:4477)]{.citex}  
    [Which deed is most enormous in the sight of Allāh?]{.trans}

### [أَيّ]{.ar} with a indefinite annexed-to noun

When the annexed-to noun of 
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is a indefinite noun, the annexation has the meaning "which" without "of".
For example,

(@) [أَيَّ شَىْءٍ كُنْتَ تَصْنَعُ]{.ar}
    [[[سنن ابن ماجه]{.ar} :2606](https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:2606)]{.citex}  
    [Which thing would you do?]{.trans}

(@) [أَيَّ شَىْءٍ نَشْتَهِي]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :1887](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1887)]{.citex}  
    [What thing shall we desire?]{.trans}

(@) [أَيُّ لَيْلَةٍ لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ]{.ar}
    [[[جامع الترمذي]{.ar} :3513](https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:3513)]{.citex}  
    [Which night is the night of Decree]{.trans}

If the annexed-to noun is a dual or plural indefinite then then inquiry is about the complete number, not just one of them.
For example:

(@) [أَيُّ رِجَالٍ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/220A]{.citex}  
    [Which men?]{.trans}

(@) [أَيُّ رَجُلَيْنِ؟]{.ar}
    [Wright 2/220A]{.citex}  
    [Which two men?]{.trans}

### Matching the rest of the question sentence with [أَيّ]{.ar}

[أَيّ]{.ar}
itself, like
[مَا]{.ar}
and
[مَنْ]{.ar},
is singular masculine.
For the purpose of
matching the rest of the question sentence with [أَيّ]{.ar},
either it can match the singular masculine to match with the word
[أَيّ]{.ar},
or 
it can match the gender and number of what
[أَيّ]{.ar}
refers to.
For example,

(@) [أَيُّ أَزْوَاجِ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم اسْتَعَاذَتْ مِنْهُ]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح البخاري]{.ar} :5254](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:5254)]{.citex}  
    [Which of the wives of the Prophet sought refuge (with Allāh) from him?]{.trans}  
    ([اسْتَعَاذَتْ]{.ar} is a feminine verb to match the feminine "wife".)

(@) [فَأَيُّ نِسَاءِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم كَانَ أَحْظَى عِنْدَهُ مِنِّي]{.ar}
    [[[صحيح مسلم]{.ar} :1423](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1423)]{.citex}  
    [So which of the women of the Prophet was dearer to him than I?]{.trans}  
    ([كَانَ]{.ar} is a masculine verb to match masculine [أَيّ]{.ar}.)

### [أَيّ]{.ar} standalone without a annexed-to noun

Occasionally, [أَيّ]{.ar} is used without a annexed-to noun.
It is then, technically, indefininte.
However, the meaning of an annexation is still implicit.
This may be when [أَيّ]{.ar} has already been used once with an an annexation,
and subsequent uses of [أَيّ]{.ar} are restricted to the previously mentioned annexation.
For example,

(@) [أَيُّ الْعَمَلِ أَحَبُّ إِلَى اللهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ؟ قَالَ الصَّلاَةُ عَلَى وَقْتِهَا، قُلْتُ ثُمَّ أَيٌّ؟]{.ar}
    [[[الأدب المفرد]{.ar} :1](https://sunnah.com/adab:1)]{.citex}  
    ['Which deed is most beloved to Allāh?' He replied, 'Prayer at its proper time.' I said, 'Then which?']{.trans}

See also section\ ... below, where [أَيّ]{.ar} is used standalone in a response.

### [أَيّ]{.ar} annexed to multiple annexed-to nouns

One [أَيّ]{.ar} may be annexed to multiple annexed-to nouns separated by [وَ]{.ar} "and".
For example,

(@) [أَيُّ زِرَاعَةِ ٱلْفَاكِهَةِ وَزِرَاعَةِ ٱلْقُطْنِ أَرْبَحُ؟]{.ar}
    [[النحو الوافي]{.ar} 3/107]{.citex}  
    [Which one of the agriculture of fruit, and the agriculture of cotton is more profitable?]{.trans}

In such a case, it is optional to have one
[أَيّ]{.ar}
or to repeat it.
So we could also say, for the same meaning:

(@) [أَيُّ زِرَاعَةِ ٱلْفَاكِهَةِ وَأَيُّ زِرَاعَةِ ٱلْقُطْنِ أَرْبَحُ؟]{.ar}

However, if one of the annexed-to nouns is an attached pronoun 
<!--for the speaker [ي]{.ar},-->
then repeating
[أَيّ]{.ar}
is mandatory.^[Wright 2/220B]
Example:

(@) [أَيِّي وَأَيُّكَ أَعْلَمُ؟]{.ar}  
    [Which one of you and me is more knowledgeable?]{.trans}

[أَيِّي وَأَيُّكَ]{.ar} is equivalent to [أَيُّنَا]{.ar} but it spells out the two options to choose from.

## Differentiating question-devices from their other functions

[[معاني النحو]{.ar} 2/37](https://shamela.ws/book/17801/420)

Many of the question-devices 
([أَ]{.ar}, [مَنْ]{.ar}, [مَا]{.ar}, [كَيْفَ]{.ar}, etc.)
also have other functions.
For example,
in chapter\ \@ref(the-connected-nouns) we learned that [مَنْ]{.ar}, [مَا]{.ar}, and [أَيّ]{.ar} are also connected nouns.
Many of the question nouns can also be used as _conditional nouns_ that we will study in chapter\ \@ref(...), if Allāh wills.

In this section, we will discuss briefly how to determine when words like
[أَ]{.ar}, [مَنْ]{.ar}, [مَا]{.ar}, [كَيْفَ]{.ar}, etc.
are question-devices, and when they could have one of their other functions.

The basic principle regarding a question sentence is that it is to be treated as one unit. 
A word from within a question sentence is not, individually, affected by anything outside the question.
Let's try to understand this using an example.

Consider the following sentence:

(@) [ٱِسْأَلْ أَيُّهُمْ قَامَ]{.ar}  
    [EisEal Eayyuhum qAm]{.trn}  
    [Ask: 'Which of them stood?']{.trans}

The speaker is commanding the addressed person to ask a group of people the question: 
"Which of them stood".

The question sentence is
[أَيُّهُمْ قَامَ]{.ar}
[Eayyuhum qAm]{.trn}
[Which of them stood]{.trans}.
This entire sentence is considered the direct doee of the verb of command [ٱسْأَلْ]{.ar} "ask!".
The question noun [أَيُّ]{.ar} [Eayyu]{.trn} is in the u-case because it is the subject of the question sentence.
It does not become [أَيَّ]{.ar} [Eayya]{.trn} in the a-case because it is not, by itself, the direct doee of 
[ٱسْأَلْ]{.ar}.
Rather, as we have just stated, the entire question sentence is the direct doee.
But because the direct doee is a sentence, and not an individual word, it does not indicate its case using, for example, an [fatHah]{.trn2} [◌َ]{.ar}.

Now, let's modify the example. Consider now this sentence:

(@) [ٱِسْأَلْ أَيَّهُمْ قَامَ]{.ar}  
    [EisEal Eayyahum qAm]{.trn}  
    [Ask the one of them who stood!]{.trans}

Now, the noun [أَيَّ]{.ar} is in the a-case because it (individually) is the direct doee of the verb of command 
[ٱسْأَلْ]{.ar}.
The speaker is now commanding the addressed person to ask (something) of only the person who stood, out of a group of people. The rest of the people are not to be asked.
Because the noun 
[أَيَّ]{.ar}
is individually affected by the preceding verb
[ٱسْأَلْ]{.ar}
it is now not a question noun, and must be one of the other functions that the word
[أَيّ]{.ar} can have.
As a matter of fact, it is here a connected noun, and the sentence following it:
[قَامَ]{.ar} "he stood" is its connecting sentence.

The other noteworthy point regarding questions
(besides their being considered one unit)
is that they may only be preceded 
either by a verb of knowledge, (like [عَلِمَ]{.ar}, [دَرىٰ]{.ar}, etc.)
or by an expression indicating that the question is being quoted.
We have already seen an example of the question being quoted in the example:

(@) [ٱِسْأَلْ أَيُّهُمْ قَامَ]{.ar}  
    [Ask: 'Which of them stood?']{.trans}

An example of a question being preceded by a verb of knowledge is:

(@) [مَا عَلِمْتُ أَذَهَبَ أَمْ مَكَثَ]{.ar}  
    [I don't know whether he went or stayed.]{.trans}

Here the question sentence is: 
[أَذَهَبَ أَمْ مَكَثَ]{.ar}
[Did he go or did he stay?]{.trans}

By the way, a question sentence may be part of a bigger question as well. For example:

(@) [أَتَدْرِي أَيُّهُمْ فِي ٱلدَّارِ؟]{.ar}  
    [EatadrI Eayyuhum fi -ddAr]{.trn}  
    [Do you know: which of them is in the house?]{.trans}  

Note now the subtle difference in meaning if we change the case of [أَيّ]{.ar} in the above example from the u-case to the a-case:

(@) [أَتَدْرِي أَيَّهُمْ فِي ٱلدَّارِ؟]{.ar}  
    [EatadrI Eayyahum fi -ddAr]{.trn}  
    [Do you know the one of them who is in the house?]{.trans}

When [أَيّ]{.ar} was in the u-case it was a question noun. And the speaker was asking the addressed person if he could figure out who, from among the group of people, was in the house.

When [أَيّ]{.ar} is in the a-case it is now a connected noun.
The connecting sentence's refer-back pronoun is omitted (as is permissible in this case, see section\ \@ref(...)). With the refer-back pronoun restored, the sentence is
[أَتَدْرِي أَيَّهُمْ هُوَ فِي ٱلدَّارِ؟]{.ar}
And the speaker is asking the addressed person if he is familiar with the person who is in the house.
Now he is not asking the addressed person to identify him, but rather if knows him as a person.

This difference is apparent with 
[أَيّ]{.ar} 
because it is a flexible noun whose case is indicated by the vowel mark at its end.
The same occurs in the other question nouns that are also connected nouns:
[مَا]{.ar}, and [مَنْ]{.ar}
but it won't often be as apparent because they are rigid nouns.

As a final note, sometimes, one of the words like 
[أَ]{.ar}, [مَنْ]{.ar}, [مَا]{.ar}, [كَيْفَ]{.ar}, etc.
may be preceded by parts of a sentence that are neither quoting, nor a verb of knowledge.
Here we can be sure that the word is not a question-device
and
must be one of its other functions. However,
it still may not be easy to figure out what that other function is.
Nevertheless, the meaning of the sentence can still usually be gleaned.
For example:

(@) [فَلْتَدْخُلْ مِنْ أَيِّ أَبْوَابِ الْجَنَّةِ شَاءَتْ]{.ar}  
    [then let her enter from whichever of the doors of paradise she wishes.]{.trans}[^question-vs-other-functions]
